tasks.q: What is a standalone computer?
a: A computer that is not connected to any other computer or network
A computer that stands on the floor rather than a desk
A computer that connects to the internet only by Wi-Fi
The main computer that controls a network
tasks.fb: A standalone computer works on its own. Its files, software and hardware can only be used on that one machine.

tasks.q: Which of these is most likely to be standalone?
a: A laptop with Wi-Fi switched off, used to write stories
A games console playing online
A smart speaker answering questions
A school PC that you log on to with your network username
tasks.fb: With Wi-Fi off and no cables, the laptop isn't connected to anything, so it is standalone. The others all rely on a network.

tasks.q: Without a network, how can you get a file onto another computer?
a: Copy it onto removable media, such as a USB stick, and carry it over
Send it by email
Save it to the cloud
Print it to the other computer
tasks.fb: Email and the cloud both need a network, so without one you have to carry the file on removable media.

tasks.q: Two friends pass one essay back and forth on a USB stick. What is the most likely problem?
a: They end up with different versions, and changes get lost
The file turns into a virus
The essay gets shorter every time it is copied
The USB stick sends it to the wrong person
tasks.fb: Every copy can be edited separately, so it is easy to lose track of which version is the latest.

tasks.q: A room has 30 standalone computers. How many printers are needed so that every computer can print directly?
a: None
tasks.fb: Each standalone computer needs its own printer plugged in, so 30 computers need 30 printers.

tasks.q: Why would needing so many printers be a problem for a school?
a: Buying, powering and maintaining lots of printers is expensive
Printers can only print one page each per day
Printers slow down the internet
Standalone printers can't print in colour
tasks.fb: More printers means more cost for the machines, ink, paper, electricity and repairs. On a network, one printer can be shared.

tasks.q: On standalone computers, how must software updates be installed?
a: Separately on every computer
Once, on a server, for every computer
Automatically by the router
They never need updating
tasks.fb: Without a network, someone has to install each update on each computer individually.

tasks.q: A standalone computer that has never been backed up has a hard drive failure. What happens to its files?
a: They are lost, because there is no other copy
They are restored from the network server
They move to the cloud automatically
They are saved on the printer
tasks.fb: There is no network, so there is no server or cloud copy. Without a backup, the files are gone.

tasks.q: Match each problem to how a network would solve it.
pairs: Save files on a file server that every computer can open
Share one printer between many computers
Install updates on every computer from one place
Back up everyone's data centrally, all at once
tasks.fb: You'll see all four of these in part 2, the school LAN.

info.title: Standalone on purpose
info.text: Some organisations deliberately keep important computers standalone, known as air-gapped, so that hackers can't reach them over a network. The trade-off is that sharing and updating become much harder.

info.title: The sneakernet
info.text: Carrying files between computers on removable media is jokingly called a sneakernet. It still happens today: some companies ship huge amounts of data on hard drives because that can be quicker than sending it over the internet.

info.title: The 3-2-1 backup rule
info.text: A common rule for backups: keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy kept somewhere else (off-site). A standalone computer with no backup breaks every part of the rule.

tasks.q: Which best describes a LAN?
a: A network covering a small area, such as one site, where the organisation owns the hardware
A network covering a large area, using connections rented from telecoms companies
A single computer not connected to anything
The cables that link countries under the sea
tasks.fb: LAN stands for local area network: small area, one site, and hardware owned by the organisation.

tasks.q: Is the Wi-Fi network in a home a LAN?
a: Yes: it covers one small site and the household owns the equipment
No: it uses Wi-Fi, so it cannot be a LAN
No: it connects to the internet, so it is a WAN
Only if more than 10 devices are connected
tasks.fb: A LAN can use cables, Wi-Fi or both. Connecting to the internet doesn't stop your home network being a LAN.

tasks.q: On a school LAN, where are shared files kept so that any computer can open them?
a: On a file server
On the router
On each student's monitor
On the switch
tasks.fb: The file server stores shared files, and the network lets every computer reach them.

tasks.q: Which of these is NOT a benefit of sharing resources on a LAN?
a: Every computer needs its own printer
One printer can be shared by a whole room
You can log on at any computer and see your own files
Files can be opened from any computer
tasks.fb: Sharing a printer is the benefit. Needing one printer per computer is the standalone problem from part 1.

tasks.q: Which of these is an advantage of a network?
a: Software can be installed and updated on every computer from one place
Viruses can spread from one computer to others
A network manager is needed to run it
Servers and switches are expensive
tasks.fb: The other three options are all disadvantages of networks.

tasks.q: How does a network make backing up easier?
a: Everyone's data is stored centrally, so it can all be backed up at once
Each computer backs itself up to a USB stick
Networks never lose data, so backups aren't needed
The switch keeps a copy of every file
tasks.fb: Central storage on a server means one backup covers everyone's work.

tasks.q: Which of these is a disadvantage of a network?
a: Viruses and malware can spread from one computer to many
Files can be shared easily
One printer can be shared
Users can communicate by email
tasks.fb: Because the computers are connected, malware on one machine can reach the others.

tasks.q: Which would best reduce the risk of a virus spreading across a school network?
a: Keep anti-malware software up to date and install security updates
Buy more printers
Use longer network cables
Turn off the file server at lunchtime
tasks.fb: Up-to-date anti-malware software and security updates stop most malware before it can spread.

tasks.q: In the LAN on this wall, which device connects all the computers together?
a: The switch
The printer
The file server
The monitor
tasks.fb: Every computer's cable runs to the switch, which links them all together.

tasks.q: Which device on this wall stores the files that everyone shares?
a: The file server
The switch
The shared printer
The cable
tasks.fb: The file server holds shared files so that any computer on the LAN can open them.

info.title: Is Wi-Fi a LAN?
info.text: A wireless LAN is sometimes called a WLAN. It is still a LAN: it covers one site and the organisation owns the equipment. Most school LANs mix cables and Wi-Fi.

info.title: Why your files follow you
info.text: When you log on at school, your username and password are checked by a server. Your documents are stored centrally, so they appear on whichever computer you use.

info.title: When malware spreads
info.text: In 2017 the WannaCry ransomware spread across networks around the world, including computers in NHS hospitals, causing cancelled appointments. It is a real example of why network security matters.

info.title: The access point above you
info.text: The disc on the ceiling is a wireless access point. It connects laptops and tablets in this room to the same LAN as the wired computers.

tasks.q: Which best describes a WAN?
a: A network covering a large geographical area that connects LANs together
A network inside one building
A network that uses no cables at all
A standalone computer with internet access
tasks.fb: WAN stands for wide area network. It covers towns, countries or the whole world, and joins LANs together.

tasks.q: A school trust links the LANs of its schools in different towns. What is this?
a: A WAN, because it covers a large area and joins LANs together
A LAN, because it all belongs to one organisation
A standalone network
It isn't a network at all
tasks.fb: Size is the key: once a network spans different towns, it is a WAN, even if one organisation runs it.

tasks.q: Who usually owns the connections used by a WAN?
a: Telecoms companies, who rent (lease) them to organisations
The school
The students
Nobody owns them
tasks.fb: Organisations rent WAN links from telecoms companies rather than building their own.

tasks.q: Why doesn't a school lay its own cable to another school 30 miles away?
a: It would cost far too much and cross land the school doesn't own, so renting a link is cheaper
Cables can't be longer than one mile
WANs never use cables
Schools aren't allowed to own any network cables
tasks.fb: Laying cable over long distances is hugely expensive and needs permission from landowners. Telecoms companies already have the cables in place.

tasks.q: What carries WAN traffic across oceans?
a: Undersea fibre optic cables
UTP cables
Bluetooth
USB cables
tasks.fb: Fibre optic cables on the seabed carry most of the internet's traffic between continents.

tasks.q: Sort each statement: does it describe a LAN or a WAN?
items: Covers towns, countries or the world
Hardware is owned by the organisation
Connections are usually rented from telecoms companies
tasks.fb: Now use these to write your three LAN bullet points and three contrasting WAN bullet points in your workbook.

tasks.q: What is the biggest WAN in the world?
a: The internet
Your school network
A home Wi-Fi network
Bluetooth
tasks.fb: The internet is a WAN of millions of connected networks.

tasks.q: Why are satellites used for some WAN links?
a: To reach places that cables can't easily reach, such as ships at sea
Because they are the cheapest option everywhere
Because they are faster than fibre in every situation
To connect computers in the same room
tasks.fb: Satellites cover remote places, but fibre is usually faster and has less delay where it is available.

info.title: Cables under the sea
info.text: Hundreds of undersea fibre optic cables carry most of the data travelling between continents. When one is damaged, traffic is rerouted along other cables, but whole regions can slow down.

info.title: Leased lines
info.text: A business that needs a fast, reliable link between its sites can rent a leased line from a telecoms company. It pays a monthly fee instead of laying its own cables.

info.title: Satellites and delay
info.text: Signals to and from satellites travel a very long way, so there is a noticeable delay called latency. That's why fibre is preferred wherever cables can reach.
